name: MedUP
summary: A smart booking and live-queue app that helps patients spend less time waiting for care.

heroImage.alt: MedUP home screen with booking, facility search and emergency shortcuts

statement.lead: MedUP brings booking, live queues and QR check-in into one calm app,
statement.rest: so patients spend less of their day waiting for care.

challenge: Getting care often starts with a wait before the wait. Patients wake early to beat the crowds, sit in traffic, hunt for parking, then arrive at a packed facility only to queue twice: once for treatment and again for their medicine.

Underneath it sits an outdated appointment and queue process with no real-time tracking, little guidance on what happens next, and no easy way to find a nearby facility. Medical staff feel it too, absorbing the frustration and planning around unpredictable crowds.

research.label: UX research
research.headline: Patients often queue twice: once for treatment, then again for their medicine.
research.problem: Getting care often means waking early, sitting in traffic and waiting at a packed facility, with no live view of the queue and no easy way to find a nearby clinic. Existing apps crashed, lost accounts or hid key features.
research.solution: A five-step booking flow that starts with the services you need, shows only real slots at nearby facilities, tracks your place in the queue live and checks you in with a QR code. Anyone can book for a parent, partner or child.

image.alt: Slot picker showing available appointment times at Ara Damansara Medical Centre

journeyMap.title: The patient journey today
journeyMap.intro: A typical visit, from deciding where to go to remembering the next appointment. The grey line is how it feels now; the teal line is the experience MedUP is designed for.
journeyMap.note: Built from the survey and benchmark findings. Thoughts are paraphrased themes, not direct quotes.

approach.title: Research
approach.body: Surveyed people who use existing health apps and benchmarked MySejahtera, Healthify and Doctor Anywhere. Users reported crashes, lost accounts, poor usability and unclear navigation. MySejahtera was strong on queue tracking but weak on usability, while the others had better interfaces but narrower features and accessibility. That gap became MedUP's opportunity.

approach.title: Map the journey
approach.body: Built a persona, mapped needs, goals and pain points, and charted the pre-improvement journey of booking an appointment to see where time and confidence were lost.

approach.title: Shape the flow
approach.body: Kept booking to five steps including confirmation. Users pick the services they need first, which narrows the facility list; nearby facilities come from their location; only genuinely available slots are shown; and anyone can book for a parent, partner or child.

approach.title: Design and prototype
approach.body: Moved from paper sketches to high-fidelity screens for the splash, homepage, appointment and services, facility and time slot, and confirmation with QR code, then linked them into a clickable Figma prototype.

journey.title: Mapping the patient journey from sign-in to check-in
body: Before designing screens, I charted how people book care today and where time and confidence were lost: finding the right facility, guessing when to leave home and waiting without knowing their place in line.
That map became the app's structure. Each group below is a tab or flow in the prototype, so a patient is never more than a few taps from booking, their queue number or their records.
goals: See the queue before you leave

walkthrough.title: Onboarding
walkthrough.subtitle: Four screens, four promises
walkthrough.body: Find a facility, book in a few taps, follow the queue live and check in with one QR code. Each screen explains one job with one illustration and a single Next button.
walkthrough.why: People in the survey abandoned health apps that felt confusing on first use. Naming the four jobs up front sets expectations before the app asks for anything personal.

images.alt: Four onboarding screens: find facilities, book appointments, real-time queue updates and QR check-in

walkthrough.title: Sign in
walkthrough.subtitle: A phone number and a one-time code
walkthrough.body: Enter a mobile number, type the code that arrives by SMS, and a clear verified state confirms the account before the app opens.
walkthrough.why: Lost accounts and forgotten passwords came up again and again. A phone number is something every patient already has, and the same number can carry appointment reminders.

images.alt: One-time code entry with a number pad

walkthrough.title: Home
walkthrough.subtitle: Three jobs, one tap away
walkthrough.body: Book an appointment, locate a facility and request an emergency sit at the top. Your next appointment and the list of services follow underneath.
walkthrough.why: Most visits start with one of three intents: book, find or get urgent help. Putting them first, with the upcoming visit always visible, means returning patients never dig through menus.

images.alt: MedUP home screen with three primary actions, the next appointment and services

walkthrough.title: Booking
walkthrough.subtitle: Service first, then place, then time
walkthrough.body: Choose who the visit is for and the service you need. The facility list narrows to places that offer it, and only open slots are shown. A progress bar tracks the four steps to confirmation.
walkthrough.why: Starting with the service removes dead ends: you never pick a clinic and then find it cannot help. Showing only real slots stops people booking times that do not exist.

images.alt: Select services step with inpatient, outpatient and emergency options
Select slot step with available times by day

walkthrough.title: Choosing a facility
walkthrough.subtitle: Everything you need on one card
walkthrough.body: Each facility card shows whether it is government or private, the address and distance, today's opening hours and how busy it is right now.
walkthrough.why: Deciding where to go was the first pain point in the journey. The crowd indicator lets patients trade a slightly longer drive for a much shorter wait.

images.alt: Select facility step listing nearby clinics
Facility card showing type, address, distance, hours and a heavy crowd indicator

walkthrough.title: Records
walkthrough.subtitle: Your history, ready to show
walkthrough.body: A medical profile with height, weight, BMI and blood type, and prescriptions with dose, route and duration, grouped under the visit they came from.
walkthrough.why: Patients repeat their history at every visit and lose track of medication. Keeping each record with its visit makes it easy to show a doctor or pharmacist in seconds.

images.alt: Medical profile with body measurements and record categories
Medication record grouped by facility visit

feature.title: Live queue and QR check-in, so you arrive when it is your turn
body: After booking, MedUP shows your queue number and the numbers being served right now, with an estimated arrival time from home.
At the facility, a single QR code handles registration, check-in and pharmacy visits.

image.alt: Booking confirmation with current queue number and a QR code to scan on arrival

style.intro: A clean clinical base of white and soft grey, with one confident teal for anything you can act on. Rounded cards and large touch targets keep every step easy to tap.

logoColor.alt: MedUP logo in teal and coral

components.intro: A small kit built for a busy clinic: large tap targets, one teal for anything you can act on, and coral kept for alerts such as crowd levels.

outcome: The first phase delivers a clickable prototype covering booking, live queue traffic for each facility, an estimated arrival time from home, medication history and past visits, upcoming-visit reminders, quick emergency contact and QR check-in.
Next steps are connecting to facilities' existing queue systems and expanding the feature set beyond this first phase.

why.title: Why it matters
why.lead: Care should start when you arrive, not hours before.
why.body: MedUP's end goal is to give patients back the time they lose to uncertainty, and to give medical staff a calmer, more predictable day.

goals.goal: Spend less of the day waiting: book in five steps, leave home when your number is close and check in with one code.
goals.measure: Time to a confirmed booking; time spent waiting at the facility

goals.goal: Book and track visits for parents, partners and children from one account.
Fewer frustrated patients and steadier crowds, as arrivals spread across the day.
goals.measure: Peak waiting-area headcount; booked visits versus walk-ins

goals.goal: Fewer no-shows and less paper at the counter.
goals.measure: No-show rate; share of check-ins by QR

why.note: These are the measures the next phase would track. The concept has not been tested with live patients yet.

impact.label: steps from opening the app to a confirmed booking

stack.title: Making it real
stack.intro: MedUP is a concept today. These are the integrations I would propose to build it, chosen to fit how Malaysian healthcare is already going digital.

items.name: MyDigital ID
items.use: Verified sign-in with Malaysia's national digital identity, alongside phone OTP, so records link safely to the right person.

items.name: HL7 FHIR R4 (MY Core)
items.use: Read appointments, records and prescriptions using the standard the Ministry of Health chose for its national Health Information Exchange.

items.name: Facility queue systems
items.use: Connect to each facility's queue and appointment system, such as HIS@KKM in public hospitals, for live 'now serving' numbers and real slots.

items.name: Google Maps Platform
items.use: Places for nearby facilities and Routes for travel time, so the app can tell you when to leave.

items.name: Push and WhatsApp
items.use: Firebase Cloud Messaging for push, and the WhatsApp Business Platform for reminders patients actually read.

items.name: DuitNow QR and FPX
items.use: Pay consultation or pharmacy fees in the app where a facility charges them.

items.name: React Native, Node.js, PostgreSQL
items.use: One app for iOS and Android, with patient data hosted in Malaysia and handled under the Personal Data Protection Act 2010.

name: MRTS Analytics Dashboard
summary: A construction progress dashboard that turns on-site data into clear, real-time decisions.

challenge: Building a rail line generates a constant stream of complex progress data from the ground. Project managers needed to see at a glance where things stood, spot risks early and act on delays, without digging through raw reports.

approach.title: Landing overview
approach.body: Colour-coded indicators flag lines approaching or past their deadlines, a built-in countdown keeps upcoming dates visible, and anything overdue turns red.

approach.title: Drill-down by package
approach.body: Selecting a line opens tabbed views for financials, resources, overall progress, safety, documents and storage, so each audience finds its own detail without clutter.

approach.title: Ground-level evidence
approach.body: A media gallery brings in on-site photos and updates captured through SitePro, connecting the numbers to what is actually happening on site.

approach.title: Safety and timeline
approach.body: Safety views track accident rates, near misses, site risk levels and compliance. Pillar progress uses four status colours (on track, completed, in progress, at risk) to keep cognitive load low.

impact.label: focused views for every work package

outcome: A dashboard that helps managers understand progress quickly, stay on schedule and make faster, better-informed decisions. The prototype is available on request.

name: SitePro
summary: A mobile-first site app for capturing daily progress right where the work happens.

challenge: Ground workers needed a quick way to report progress from site. Reports had to be accurate, timely and structured, because they feed the central dashboard that project managers and senior management rely on.

approach.title: Sign-in and sites
approach.body: A clean sign-in leads to a landing page listing every active project, so workers can switch between sites in one tap.

approach.title: Calendar-based reports
approach.body: Daily reports live on a calendar, making past days easy to revisit, with a single plus button to add or update today's entry.

approach.title: Detail without friction
approach.body: Each report captures resource usage, progress metrics, notes and photos through quick, multi-purpose inputs, keeping data entry fast on a busy site.

outcome: SitePro bridges on-site activity and high-level monitoring: everything submitted flows straight into the MRTS analytics dashboard. The prototype is available on request.

name: SavvySpend
summary: A calendar-first budgeting app for planning, tracking and paying monthly commitments.

challenge: Subscriptions, car loans, mortgages and savings goals all fall due on different days, which makes a month's commitments hard to see in one place. The goal was a bird's-eye view of what is due and what is paid, simple enough for newcomers to finance apps yet useful for tech-savvy users.

approach.title: The calendar as the hub
approach.body: Every commitment sits on a full-screen calendar, which also makes month-to-month comparison easy.

approach.title: Lightweight adding
approach.body: New items open in a drawer sheet rather than a full page: name, due date, amount, who to pay, reminder and payment method.

approach.title: Smart details
approach.body: Tapping a date shows one item's details directly or a list when several are due, and each item switches between paid and unpaid in one tap.

approach.title: A calm palette
approach.body: A greenish-yellow 'Parchment' primary colour suggests growth, stability and prosperity, and onboarding stays short.

outcome: A full-flow, high-fidelity Figma prototype covering splash, onboarding, the home overview (this month, an automatic expense breakdown, upcoming payments and paid transactions), adding items and viewing them.
Future ideas include categories, recurring payments and custom notes.

name: E-Leave
summary: A mobile leave app that replaces paper forms and clunky web portals with a quick request flow.

challenge: Applying for leave through a paper form or a website-only system is a hassle for employees and HR alike.

approach.title: Sketch
approach.body: Started on paper to lay the foundations of the app quickly.

approach.title: Low fidelity
approach.body: Rebuilt the sketches in Figma to understand the flows and the experience end to end.

approach.title: High fidelity
approach.body: Designed a polished prototype, including ideas to encourage early sign-up by highlighting member benefits.

outcome: A low- and high-fidelity prototype. The project is in an exploratory phase, with no-code tools such as FlutterFlow or Glide under consideration for a build.

name: GIS with JPS Selangor
client: Department of Irrigation and Drainage (JPS) Selangor
summary: Mapping catchment terrain and processing drone surveys alongside engineers at JPS Selangor.

challenge: Engineers and quantity surveyors planning construction and consultancy work needed clear terrain and river-flow pictures of their project areas. Under the guidance of the Deputy Director, I applied GIS to JPS projects for testing, analysis and presentation.

approach.title: Outline the catchment
approach.body: Traced the Ulu Yam catchment in Hulu Langat in Google Earth Pro, where the Anak Sungai Liam tributary feeds Sungai Liam and then Sungai Selangor, and exported it as KML/KMZ.

approach.title: Convert and analyse
approach.body: Converted the data to GPX and into ArcMap features, interpolated elevation with IDW, generated contour lines, then layered the river and boundary data and masked it to the working area.

approach.title: Fly and process
approach.body: Trained with JPS and DJI on the Phantom 4 Pro V2.0, flew an automated mission at Kuala Perlis, and processed the images in Pix4DMapper into an orthomosaic, a digital surface model and a dense 3D point cloud.

impact.label: drone images processed into a 3D survey
source elevation of the Anak Sungai Liam, mapped

outcome: An elevation and contour map of the Ulu Yam catchment that helps contractors, geographers and engineers plan construction, plus drone survey outputs for Kuala Perlis, and hands-on experience in drone photogrammetry.
